title: Abbas ibn Firnas
hook: a craftsman of Cordoba who, the reports say, strapped on wings and jumped

segments.voice: Yesterday: caliph, the title Abd al-Rahman the Third took for Cordoba. Your line was: a western caliphate, a golden age with a bill.

A man stands on a high place near Cordoba. Feathers are fastened over his body, and a pair of wings is tied to his arms. People have come out to watch. He leans forward, and he jumps. That's how a later historian of al-Andalus, al-Maqqari, tells it, passing on what earlier writers said they saw. The man glides for a stretch, the report says, the way a bird does. Then he comes down hard, and hurts his back. His name was Abbas ibn Firnas.
screen: `FEATHERS AND A PAIR OF WINGS.` → `HE JUMPS.` → `HE COMES DOWN HARD.`

segments.voice: Who was he? In the reports, a man of the Cordoba court with many crafts at once: poetry, music, the stars, the making of instruments. The same writers credit him with work on glass made from stone, and a model of the sky built in his own house. Take those as the reports give them, admiring and a little larger than life. Now the birds. The Qur'an keeps sending its listeners outside to look. In Pickthall's translation: "Have they not seen the birds above them spreading out their wings and closing them?" The verse goes on: nothing holds them up except the Beneficent. So looking up at a bird, in this tradition, is already a kind of reading. Abbas looked, and then he tried. Why did he land so badly? The report's answer is oddly specific. He had forgotten that birds come down on their tails, so he never made himself one. He studied the wing and missed the tail. A very human mistake: you copy the part you admire and skip the part that looks boring. One honest caution. This is a story told long after, by a writer gathering older accounts. Some readers take it nearly as written; others wonder how much grew in the telling. Either way, it keeps a man who wondered about birds, built something, jumped, got hurt, and left behind a lesson about tails. He tried to fly.
screen: `A MAN OF MANY CRAFTS.` · `HAVE THEY NOT SEEN THE BIRDS?` · `HE FORGOT THE TAIL.` · `A REPORT, TOLD LONG AFTER.` · then, large: `HE TRIED TO FLY.`

segments.voice: Pick one small thing you've never tried, a dish, a stretch, a phrase in another language, and picture only the first step. Then ask the Abbas question: what's my tail, the dull part I'm likely to skip? Muslims often say bismillah, in the name of God, before beginning something; if you pray, you can begin with it, and if you don't, just hold the first step in mind.
At-tayr. Arabic for the birds, the Qur'an's call to look up, which Abbas ibn Firnas answered by putting on wings, jumping, gliding, and landing hard for want of a tail. Today's word.
Your line: he tried to fly. Even the hard landing taught him something. Until next time.

howItsDone: Abbas ibn Firnas is remembered as an inventor of al-Andalus, and his attempted flight is known mainly through the account passed on by the historian al-Maqqari.
